The drug information provided is based on FDA package inserts, the National Library of Medicine, and clinical guidelines or consensus statements. WikiDoc does not endorse the use of any medication or device inconsistent with its labeling. Common adverse reactions to potassium iodide include stomach upset, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, skin rash, swelling or tenderness of salivary glands, gastrointestinal bleeding, and confusion. Less frequent side effects may include irregular heartbeat, numbness, tingling, pain or weakness in extremities, unusual tiredness, leg heaviness, fever, and swelling of the neck or throat. Thyroid adenoma, goiter, and myxedema are also possible. Chronic iodine poisoning (iodism) may occur with prolonged use or high doses, presenting as burning of the mouth or throat, severe headache, metallic taste, gum soreness, cold-like symptoms, eye irritation with eyelid swelling, increased salivation, acne-like skin lesions, and rarely, severe skin eruptions. If iodism symptoms appear, the drug should be discontinued, and supportive therapy provided. For adults, potassium iodide is indicated as an expectorant in chronic pulmonary diseases with thick mucus, such as bronchial asthma, bronchitis, and pulmonary emphysema. The recommended dose is 6 mL (600 mg) diluted in water, fruit juice, or milk, taken 3 to 4 times daily with food or milk to reduce gastric irritation. The medication should not be used longer than necessary to achieve the desired effect. Off-label adult use includes inducing thyroid involution before surgery, with a dose of 60–250 mg orally three times daily for 10 days. Pediatric indications and dosages are limited in the drug label, and safety and effectiveness in children have not been established. Off-label pediatric use is also limited in information. Potassium iodide is contraindicated in patients with known sensitivity to iodides. It can cause fetal harm, abnormal thyroid function, and goiter when administered to pregnant women. Pregnant patients should be informed of these risks. Adverse reactions reported in clinical trials include stomach upset, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, skin rash, and salivary gland swelling or tenderness. Less common reactions include gastrointestinal bleeding, confusion, irregular heartbeat, numbness, tingling, pain or weakness in extremities, unusual tiredness, leg heaviness, fever, and neck or throat swelling. Chronic iodine poisoning (iodism) may occur with prolonged treatment or high doses, and symptoms typically resolve after discontinuation of the drug. Adequate fluid and salt intake can help eliminate iodide. Potassium iodide may interact with other medications. Concurrent use with lithium or antithyroid drugs can enhance hypothyroid and goitrogenic effects. Use with potassium-containing medications, potassium-sparing diuretics, or ACE inhibitors may lead to hyperkalemia and cardiac arrhythmias or arrest. Potassium iodide is excreted in breast milk and may cause skin rash and thyroid suppression in nursing infants. There is no established FDA guidance on its use during labor, delivery, or in specific populations such as geriatric, gender, racial, renal, hepatic, or immunocompromised patients. Acute toxicity from potassium iodide is rare but may include angioedema, laryngeal edema, and cutaneous hemorrhages. Symptoms of iodism typically resolve after stopping the drug, and fluid and salt intake can aid in elimination. Potassium iodide acts as an expectorant by increasing respiratory tract secretions and reducing mucus viscosity. It should be stored at controlled room temperature (15–30°C or 59–86°F) in tightly closed, light-resistant containers. If the solution crystallizes in cold temperatures, warming and shaking can redissolve the crystals. However, if the solution turns brownish-yellow, it should be discarded.
